ref: Homily 20 on Hebrews, section 3 (NPNF1-14 numbering), comment on Heb 10:28
quote_en: He that has despised Moses' law dies without mercy, under two or three witnesses. Without mercy, he says; so that there is no pardon, no pity there although the law is of Moses; for he ordained the most of it. What is under two or three? If two or three bore witness, he means, they immediately suffered punishment.
quote_orig: [Ἀ]θετήσας γὰρ, φησὶ, τις νόμον Μωϋσέως, χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν ἐπὶ δυσὶν ἢ τρισὶ μάρτυσιν ἀποθνήσκει. Χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν, φησίν. Ὥστε οὐδεμία συγγνώμη, οὐδεὶς ἔλεος ἐκεῖ· καίτοιγε Μωϋσέως ὁ νόμος ἐστί. [Greek OCR of the sentence 'If two or three bore witness…' is cut off in the OCR at 'ἐὐθέως τὴν'.]
from_: He that has despised Moses' law dies
keys: dies without mercy
no pardon, no pity there although the law is of Moses
they immediately suffered punishment
context: Chrysostom comments on Heb 10:26-31, where the writer warns those who sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth. For v.28 he explains the Mosaic penalty as a historical fact: under the Law, when two or three witnesses testified, the guilty 'immediately suffered punishment'. He does not say that Christians must carry out that penalty; the comparison he draws comes in the next passage.
caveat: Gardiner's translation; Scripture markers stripped from the quotation; Greek is OCR from Field (1862) with visible OCR errors corrected in brackets. Text is a preached homily recorded in notes (see works.json).

ref: Homily 20 on Hebrews, section 3, comment on Heb 10:29 (the 'sorer punishment') and its application
quote_en: Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who has trodden under foot the Son of God and has counted the blood of the covenant an unholy [a common] thing, and has done despite unto the Spirit of grace? And how does a man tread under foot the Son of God? When partaking of Him in the mysteries (he would say) he has wrought sin, has he not trodden Him under foot? Has he not despised Him? For just as we make no account of those who are trodden under foot, so also, they who sin have made no account of Christ; and so they have sinned. You are become the Body of Christ, and givest you yourself to the devil, so that he treads you under foot.
quote_orig: Πόσῳ δοκεῖτε χείρονος ἀξιωθήσεται τιμωρίας ὁ τὸν [υἱ]ὸν τοῦ θεοῦ καταπατήσας, καὶ τὸ αἷμα τῆς διαθήκης κοινὸν ἡγησάμενος, καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς χάριτος ἐνυβρίσας. … Καὶ πῶς καταπατεῖ τις τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ; Ὅταν γὰρ αὐτοῦ μετέχων ἐν τοῖς μυστηρίοις, ἁμαρτίαν ἐργάσηται, φησὶν, οὐχὶ κατεπάτησεν αὐτόν; [OCR; 'νὸν' corrected to υἱὸν; the middle of the paragraph is not transcribed.]
from_: Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye,
to: so that he treads you under foot.
keys: Of how much sorer punishment
You are become the Body of Christ
so that he treads you under foot
context: He reads 'trampling under foot the Son of God' as sinning while partaking of the mysteries, and applies the whole warning to the baptized who sin. The 'sorer punishment' itself is not specified in this section. Chrysostom calls it 'more fearful' than being trampled by dogs (Matt 7:6), and says the verse 'appears to me to hint at the mysteries'. He does not name a human penalty. Compare chr_x_heb20_excommunication (section 1).
caveat: Shows that he applies Heb 10:29 to baptized Christians, not to heretics. Does not say the penalty is to be executed by Christians. Greek OCR.

ref: Homily 20 on Hebrews, section 2, comment on Heb 10:27 ('the adversaries')
quote_en: By Adversaries he means not the unbelievers, but those also who do what is against virtue; or [else he means] that the same fire shall receive them of the household also, which [receives] the adversaries.
quote_orig: Ὑπεναντίους οὐ τοὺς ἐ[?] Ἄλλοις φησὶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἐναντία πράττοντας τῇ ἀρετῇ [OCR: the word before 'Ἄλλοις' is garbled; the sense 'not only outsiders but also those who act against virtue' fits the English].
from_: By Adversaries he means not the
keys: By Adversaries he means not the unbelievers
those also who do what is against virtue
fire shall receive them of the household also
context: Heb 10:27 speaks of 'a certain fearful looking for of judgment, and fiery indignation which shall devour the adversaries'. Chrysostom says the adversaries are not only outsiders (unbelievers) but also those who act against virtue, so the warning reaches insiders. He offers a second reading ('or [else he means]') that the same fire also receives 'them of the household'.
caveat: The English says 'not the unbelievers ... but ... also'; the Greek OCR ('not those from others, but also those ...') carries the same 'not only X but also Y' sense. Two readings are given. The homily does not say how this fire is applied in human hands.

ref: Homily 13 on Hebrews, comment on Heb 7:19 ('the Law made nothing perfect')
quote_en: For written precepts were there set down, Do this and Do not that, being enjoined only, and not giving power within. But the Hope is not such. What is a disannulling? A casting out. A disannulling is a disannulling of things which are of force. So that he implied, that it [once] was of force, but henceforward was of no account, since it accomplished nothing. Was the Law then of no use? It was indeed of use; and of great use: but to make men perfect it was of no use. For in this respect he says, The Law made nothing perfect. All were figures, all shadows; circumcision, sacrifice, sabbath.
quote_orig: Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐτελείωσεν ὁ νόμος. … Γράμματα γὰρ ἦν κείμενα, τόδε πρᾶττε, καὶ τόδε μὴ πρᾶττε, ὑποτιθέμενα μόνον, οὐχὶ καὶ δύναμιν ἐντιθέντα. Ἡ δὲ ἐλπὶς οὐ τοιαύτη. [OCR; the middle of the passage is not transcribed; 'ἐντιθέντα' corrected from OCR.]
from_: For written precepts were there set
keys: being enjoined only, and not giving power within
The Law made nothing perfect
All were figures, all shadows
context: Heb 7:19 says 'the Law made nothing perfect'. Chrysostom explains that written precepts ('Do this and Do not that') were enjoined but gave no inner power, and that the Law was 'of use; and of great use' but could not make men perfect. Circumcision, sacrifice and the sabbath are 'figures' and 'shadows' that pass away. This is the closest he comes to a contrast between the Law and the Gospel's fullness.
caveat: He says the Law 'was indeed of use; and of great use', so this is not a condemnation of the Law as evil. The 'perfect' is about power to make men perfect, not about moral content. Greek OCR; the New Advent text has a typo ('There fore'), not quoted.

ref: Homily 17 on Matthew, comment on Matt 5:31-32 (divorce; the Mosaic permission)
quote_en: For this cause He allowed the less, to remove the greater evil. For that this was not a primary law, hear Him saying, Moses wrote these things according to the hardness of your hearts, that you might not slay them in the house, but rather put them out.
from_: For this cause He allowed the less,
keys: He allowed the less, to remove the greater evil
this was not a primary law
according to the hardness of your hearts
context: In the Matthew 5 discussion of divorce, Chrysostom says Moses' permission was a lesser concession, 'the less', to remove a greater evil, and he cites the words 'according to the hardness of your hearts'. He then says Christ 'is enforcing, not overthrowing' the older law, but 'perfecting, not doing them away'.
caveat: The concession is about a specific practice (divorce) and the phrase 'slay them in the house' refers to wives, not to heretics. Greek not read.

ref: Homily 18 on Matthew, comment on Matt 5:38-40 ('an eye for an eye')
quote_en: But if any one accuses the ancient law, because it commands such retaliation, he seems to me very unskillful in the wisdom that becomes a legislator, and ignorant of the virtue of opportunities, and the gain of condescension. For if he considered who were the hearers of these sayings, and how they were disposed, and when they received this code of laws, he will thoroughly admit the wisdom of the Lawgiver, and will see that it is one and the same, who made both those laws and these, and who wrote each of them exceeding profitably, and in its due season. Yes, for if at the beginning He had introduced these high and most weighty commandments, men would not have received either these, or the others; but now ordaining them severally in their due time, He has by the two corrected the whole world.
from_: But if any one accuses the ancient
to: by the two corrected the whole world.
keys: in its due season
if at the beginning He had introduced these high and most weighty commandments
He has by the two corrected the whole world
context: Chrysostom answers the critics of 'an eye for an eye': the same Lawgiver gave the older rule and the higher precepts, each 'in its due season'. He argues that had He given the high commandments at the beginning, people would have rejected them, so the commandments were ordered over time to correct the whole world.
caveat: This is an argument from pedagogy, not a statement that Christians may never use penalties. In the same homily he also says that retaliation is what 'the abstract nature of justice demands' (see chr_x_matt16_eyeforeye). Greek not read.

ref: Homily 46 on Matthew, section 1 (NPNF1-10), comment on Matt 13:28-30 (the tares)
quote_en: For it is not right to put a heretic to death, since an implacable war would be brought into the world. By these two reasons then He restrains them; one, that the wheat be not hurt; another, that punishment will surely overtake them, if incurably diseased.
quote_orig: … ὅτι ὥσπε δεῖ ἀναιρεῖν αἱρετικόν· ἐπεὶ πόλεμος ἄσπονδος ἔμελλεν … [OCR of PG 58, two-column interleaved. The negative 'οὐ' that the English requires seems dropped by OCR ('ὥσπε' for 'ὥσπερ οὐ'?); verify against print.]
from_: For it is not right to put a heretic
keys: it is not right to put a heretic to death
an implacable war would be brought into the world
punishment will surely overtake them
context: The servants offer to gather up the tares; the householder forbids it. Chrysostom says the Master forbids putting heretics to death, for two reasons: the wheat would be hurt, and an implacable war would follow. The 'punishment' that will overtake the heretics is the judgment at the harvest, not a human sentence.
caveat: The prohibition is specifically on killing, not on all restraint: the very next passage (chr_x_matt46_checking) says the same homily allows restraining heretics. Greek OCR fragments only.

ref: Against the Jews (Adversus Iudaeos), Homily 1, section 9
quote_en: Since you are the army of Christ, be overly careful in searching to see if anyone favoring an alien faith has mingled among you, and make his presence know-not so that we may put him to death as those generals did, nor that we may punish him or take our vengeance upon him, but that we may free him from his error and ungodliness and make him entirely our own.
from_: Since you are the army of Christ,
to: and make him entirely our own.
keys: so that we may put him to death as those generals did
nor that we may punish him or take our vengeance upon him
free him from his error and ungodliness
context: Chrysostom addresses the congregation about members who favor 'an alien faith'. He compares the Church with the Roman army, in which generals executed soldiers who favored the Persians, and rejects that model: the aim is to free such people from their error, not to kill or punish them.
caveat: The source reads 'know-not' (likely 'known—not'); the quotation keeps the page's wording. The next section (chr_x_advjud1_s10) threatens concealers with 'the same penalty'. Translation of unknown origin, posted as public domain. Greek not read.

ref: Homily 46 on Matthew, section 1, comment on Matt 13:28-30
quote_en: Either He means this, If you are to take up arms, and to kill the heretics, many of the saints also must needs be overthrown with them; or that of the very tares it is likely that many may change and become wheat. If therefore ye root them up beforehand, you injure that which is to become wheat, slaying some, in whom there is yet room for change and improvement. He does not therefore forbid our checking heretics, and stopping their mouths, and taking away their freedom of speech, and breaking up their assemblies and confederacies, but our killing and slaying them.
quote_orig: Οὐ τοίνυν κατέχειν αἱρετικοὺς, καὶ ἐπιστομίζειν, καὶ ἐκκόπτειν αὐτῶν τὴν παῤῥησίαν, … τὰς σπονδὰς διαλύειν χωλύει, ἀλλ' ἀναιρεῖν … [OCR, two-column interleaved; fragments only.]
from_: Either He means this, If you are
to: but our killing and slaying them.
keys: He does not therefore forbid our checking heretics
stopping their mouths, and taking away their freedom of speech
breaking up their assemblies and confederacies
context: Right after the prohibition on killing, Chrysostom explains that the Lord forbids the killing of heretics but not their 'checking', silencing them, restricting their freedom of speech, or breaking up their assemblies. He reads the prohibition as covering only killing and slaying, not the other measures.
caveat: ADVERSE. This is the most important adverse text for this Father: he approves coercive measures against heretics short of death (restricting speech, dissolving assemblies). It does not mention fines or exile in this passage. Greek is OCR with interleaving.

ref: Homily 16 on Matthew, comment on the Old Law's 'eye for an eye' (Matt 5:38 range)
quote_en: For He made this law, not that we might strike out one another's eyes, but that fear of suffering by others might restrain us from doing any such thing to them. As therefore He threatened the Ninevites with overthrow, not that He might destroy them, (for had that been His will, He ought to have been silent), but that He might by fear make them better, and so quiet His wrath: so also has He appointed a punishment for those who wantonly assail the eyes of others, that if good principle dispose them not to refrain from such cruelty, fear may restrain them from injuring their neighbors' sight.
from_: For He made this law, not that
to: restrain them from injuring their neighbors' sight.
keys: fear of suffering by others might restrain us
so also has He appointed a punishment for those who wantonly assail the eyes of others
fear may restrain them from injuring their neighbors' sight
context: Against critics who call the Old Law's retaliation cruel, Chrysostom says God made the law so that fear of punishment would restrain men, as He threatened the Ninevites. In the next paragraph he compares the law's penalty to a 'strong chain' on the wicked, 'who detains those assassins in prison'.
caveat: ADVERSE in principle: he approves punishment (including the Law's own penalties) as legitimate restraint. It does not name heretics, and the penalty is the Mosaic one, not a call for the Church to impose it. Greek not read.

ref: Homily 20 on Hebrews, section 1, comment on Heb 10:26 (the 'willful sin')
quote_en: If then thou return to your former vomit, there awaits you on the other hand excommunication and fire and whatever such things there are. For there is no second sacrifice.
from_: If then thou return to your former
to: For there is no second sacrifice.
keys: excommunication and fire
For there is no second sacrifice
context: Addressing baptized people ('You were cleansed; ... you have become a son'), Chrysostom says that if they return to their former sins, 'there awaits you ... excommunication and fire'. He also says there is no second sacrifice, no second 'Washing', but repentance remains.
caveat: BORDERLINE. The penalty threatened is ecclesiastical (excommunication) plus the fire of judgment; it is not civil or capital punishment, and he does not describe its enforcement. Included because excommunication of apostates is a form of coercion the team should know about. Greek not located in the OCR.

quote_en: If you are unwilling to do this, if you know of such a person but conceal him, be sure that both you and he will be subject to the same penalty.

keys: both you and he will be subject to the same penalty
if you know of such a person but conceal him
context: Continuing section 9, Chrysostom says that whoever knows of such a person and conceals him will share the same penalty, and cites Paul's words that those who approve wickedness are also liable.
caveat: BORDERLINE. The 'penalty' is not specified, and it is not stated who would impose it (God, or the Church, or the state). The text is rhetorical exhortation. Greek not read.

quote_en: Although such beasts are unfit for work, they are fit for killing. And this is what happened to the Jews: while they were making themselves unfit for work, they grew fit for slaughter. This is why Christ said: "But as for these my enemies, who did not want me to be king over them, bring them here and slay them".
from_: Although such beasts are unfit for work,
to: bring them here and slay them".
keys: they are fit for killing
they grew fit for slaughter
bring them here and slay them
context: Chrysostom describes the Jews with animal metaphors (unfit for work, fit for killing) and presents their 'slaughter' as the result of their own conduct, quoting Christ's words 'bring them here and slay them' about 'these my enemies'. The source does not cite the verse, but the wording is that of the parable of the nobles (Luke 19:27).
caveat: ADVERSE rhetoric about Jews rather than heretics. The violent words are attributed to Christ, as judgment on those who rejected him; the text does not name a human agent or call for human violence. Greek not read.
